title: Spiritual Warfare: A Bible Study on the Unseen Battle
subtitle: A five-session study on the powers, the armor, and the war we cannot see.
summary:
This study is for Christians who suspect that the New Testament means something real when it says our fight is not against flesh and blood, and who are tired of choosing between two bad options, the church that finds a demon behind every bush and the church that has quietly stopped believing in the devil at all. It walks slowly through five sessions on the biblical worldview of the powers, on the armor of God read piece by piece, on temptation and the flesh that names the enemy within and not only the enemy without, on the victory already won at the cross where Christ disarmed the powers, and on the ordinary means by which ordinary Christians stand, prayer and Scripture and the gathered church and the table. It is built so a busy small group or a volunteer can lead it with no preparation. Every question carries the answer behind it. Every silence has a backup. Every session ends in prayer.

This is not a study that stands above the battle and reports on it. The writer came to faith out of atheism, which means he once held the materialist account of evil with both hands and knows its pull from the inside, the reasonable conviction that there is nothing behind the world but atoms and accidents. He also pastors real people and has watched things in a counseling room that the atoms do not explain. He writes from between the two errors C. S. Lewis named, the disbelief that flatters the enemy and the obsession that does the same. He will not sell you a war story to thrill you, and he will not talk you out of a war the Scriptures plainly describe. The one thing he refuses, on every page, is the sensational reading that turns a Christian into a frightened person scanning the room for spirits. The battle is real. The victory is already decided. And the weapons handed to the ordinary believer are almost embarrassingly plain, a belt, a shield, a book, a prayer, a shared loaf. This study means to put them in your hands.
audience: Christians, small groups, and anyone unsure what to make of the New Testament's language of the powers

sessions.title: The World Behind the World
sessions.aim: To recover the biblical worldview of the powers, past both the superstition that names a demon behind every bush and the materialism that denies there is anything behind the world at all, and to see that the New Testament describes a real war on a wider front than either error can hold.
sessions.summary: A young man once told Bell, in the patient tone people save for a slow child, that he had outgrown the devil around the same age he outgrew Santa Claus, that no thinking adult believes in a horned thing with a pitchfork, that evil is only the gap between our biology and our ideals. Bell did not argue. He asked where the twentieth century came from, the one that industrialized killing and filed it under policy, and watched the confidence drain out of the sentence. The real question is not whether there are cartoon devils, there are not, but what account of evil is large enough to hold what human beings actually do. Most of us are running on one of two answers and both are too small. The first is superstition, the world where a flat tire is an attack and every bad mood is an oppression and every hard thing wears a spirit's name. The second is materialism, the world with no behind at all, only atoms and accidents, where evil is a word we will eventually explain away. Scripture refuses both. It says plainly that we do not wrestle against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities and cosmic powers over this present darkness, and it also refuses to let us become people who see nothing else. Bell takes the strong case for the sober reading, that overheated warfare talk has made Christians superstitious and afraid, and grants it fully. He takes the strong case for the charismatic reading, that the modern West has simply stopped believing what the apostles believed, and grants that too. Then the turn. The powers are real, both personal and woven into the structures that outlive the people who serve them, and the war is being fought whether or not you have noticed you are in it.

keyScripture.why: For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places, naming the real front of the battle in a way that rules out both the person who sees no war and the person who sees only demons.

discussion.q: Bell says most of us are running on one of two accounts of evil, superstition or materialism, and both are too small. Before tonight, which one had more grip on you, and where did you get it?
discussion.behind: Surface the default before defining anything. Some in the room grew up seeing a demon behind every setback, some absorbed the modern conviction that there is nothing behind the world at all, and most carry a quiet mix of both. The point is not to settle which is right yet, only to expose the water each person has been swimming in, because you cannot examine an assumption you have not first named.

discussion.q: Paul says we do not wrestle against flesh and blood. When you are in real conflict, with a person, a habit, an institution, how often do you actually believe there is anything behind the flesh and blood in front of you?
discussion.behind: Press on the gap between the doctrine and the instinct. Most Christians affirm the verse and then live as practical materialists, treating every conflict as purely human. The aim is to help the room feel how rarely the unseen enters their reckoning, not to make them paranoid but to make them honest about how small their working world has become.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for the sober reading, that overheated warfare talk has made Christians superstitious and afraid. What is true in that warning, and where have you seen the excess it is worried about?
discussion.behind: Protect the even-handedness from the start. The sober critique is right that fear-driven, demon-hunting Christianity has done real harm, has excused laziness, and has frightened people out of responsibility. Let the room name the excess honestly before the session insists the war is nonetheless real. Do not let sobriety curdle into unbelief.

discussion.q: Bell also takes the strong case for the reading that says the modern West has simply stopped believing what the apostles plainly believed. What would it cost you to take the New Testament's account of the powers as seriously as it takes itself?
discussion.behind: Now press the other side. The materialist reflex is so deep in educated people that the apostles' plain speech about the powers gets quietly translated into metaphor. Ask the room to sit with the possibility that Paul meant what he said, and that our embarrassment is a cultural inheritance, not a discovery. Keep it curious, not scolding.

discussion.q: Bell says the war is being fought whether or not you have noticed you are in it. Where in your life this year might a battle have been going on that you filed entirely under ordinary trouble?
discussion.behind: Move from theory to the particular. Not every hard thing is an attack, and the leader should say so, but the person who never once considers the unseen has adopted the materialist frame without noticing. Invite honest reflection on a season of temptation, discouragement, or division that may have had more behind it than the surface showed, without manufacturing drama.

objections.objection: Talk of demons and dark powers is exactly the kind of prescientific superstition that keeps people from taking real responsibility. Blame the devil and you never have to fix the system, the addiction, or yourself.
objections.response: Grant the danger, because it is real and the Scriptures share the concern. A faith that blames a spirit for every failure has found a way to never repent, and the New Testament never once lets a person off the hook by pointing at the devil. When Paul lists the works of the flesh he does not say a demon made you do it, he says these came out of you. So take the responsibility with full seriousness. But notice that naming the powers does not remove human responsibility in Scripture, it sits alongside it. The same Bible that says each person is tempted by his own desire also says the tempter is real, and holds both without strain. The mature reading is not either the devil or me, it is that my sin is genuinely mine and there is also an enemy who works the field I have already left unguarded. Refusing the superstition does not require you to adopt the materialism. It requires you to grow up into a world with more in it than atoms and less in it than a demon behind every bush.

objections.objection: I am a rational person. I cannot make myself believe in invisible spiritual beings just because a first-century text assumes them. That is asking me to switch off my mind.
objections.response: Honor the honesty, because it is the writer's own former position and he will not pretend otherwise. He came to faith out of atheism, and he knows from the inside how reasonable the closed world feels, how obvious it seems that there is nothing behind the visible. But notice what the closed world has never managed to account for. It cannot explain the surplus in human evil, the way atrocity so often exceeds every rational motive, as if something were being served beyond the calculating self. It cannot explain why the century most confident that it had outgrown the devil produced the most efficient horrors in human history. The point is not to frighten you back into a medieval cosmos, it is to ask whether the modern account is actually large enough for the data, or whether we called it maturity when we simply stopped looking. You do not have to switch off your mind to believe the New Testament here. You have to be willing to suspect that your mind was handed a map with a whole country left off it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which error do you actually live inside, the one that sees a demon behind every hard thing, or the one that has quietly decided there is nothing behind anything, and what has that error cost you?
sessions.practice: This week, when you hit a genuine conflict, a temptation that seems to arrive from nowhere, a division in your family or church that keeps outrunning its stated cause, pause before you assign it entirely to flesh and blood. Do not go hunting for spirits, and do not excuse anyone, including yourself. Simply ask whether there might be more behind it than the surface shows, and pray accordingly. Write down what changes in how you pray when you stop assuming the visible is the whole field.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, you made a world with more in it than we can see, and we have shrunk it down to what fits our instruments. Some of us made it superstitious, jumping at shadows and blaming a spirit for what our own hands did. Some of us made it flat, with nothing behind it at all, and called our unbelief maturity. Forgive us both errors. Open our eyes to the real war without frightening us, and steady us in the responsibility that is genuinely ours. Teach us to see the world you actually made, wider than the materialist allows and simpler than the sensationalist fears, and to stand in it unafraid because you already hold it. Amen.
reflection: Which of the two errors, the superstitious or the materialist, has had the quieter and deeper grip on how I actually live?
Do I really believe Paul when he says my hardest conflicts are not finally against flesh and blood, or do I affirm it on Sunday and forget it by Monday?
Where have I either excused my own sin by blaming an enemy, or dismissed a real enemy by explaining everything as ordinary trouble?
sessions.teaching: A young man once told Bell, in the patient tone people reserve for a slow child, that he had outgrown the devil at about the same age he outgrew Santa Claus. No thinking adult, he said, believes in a horned creature with a pitchfork, and evil is only the gap between our biology and our ideals, a problem of wiring and upbringing that better conditions will eventually close. Bell did not argue. He asked the young man where he thought the twentieth century had come from, the century that industrialized murder and filed it under policy, that built the machinery of the camps with engineers and timetables and a clear conscience, and he watched the confidence drain out of the sentence. We begin there, because the real question is not whether there are cartoon devils. There are not. The question is whether any of us actually holds an account of evil large enough for what human beings demonstrably do, and most of us do not. Most of us are running on one of two answers, and both are too small. The first answer is superstition. It is the world where a flat tire is an attack and a bad mood is an oppression, where every hard thing has a spirit's name on it and the Christian life becomes a nervous scan of the room for the enemy's fingerprints. This reading flatters the devil by seeing him everywhere, and it excuses the sinner by locating the trouble anywhere but in his own chest. The second answer is materialism. It is the world with no behind at all, only atoms and accidents and the misfiring of a frightened primate brain, where evil is a placeholder word we will one day replace with better neuroscience. This reading flatters the modern self by making it the top of the cosmos, and it has quietly become the working faith of a great many Christians who would never say so out loud. Scripture will not let us keep either one. It says, in the plainest words Paul owns, that we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. That single verse cuts both errors at once. It tells the materialist that the visible is not the whole field, that there is a behind to the world after all. And it tells the superstitious man that the war is fought at the level of rulers and authorities and structures, not at the level of every stubbed toe, that the front is wider and stranger than his demon-behind-every-bush cosmos allows. Take the strong case for the sober reading first, because it deserves a real hearing and it is often right. It says that overheated warfare talk has made Christians afraid and superstitious, that the deliverance industry has sold fear and excused laziness, that a person forever binding spirits over a traffic jam has never once done the harder work of repentance. All of that is true, and Bell grants every word of it. He has watched fear-driven Christianity do real damage, has seen people paralyzed by a cosmos of lurking enemies, and he will not add to it. Now take the strong case for the other reading, because it is also right about something the sober reading tends to lose. It says the modern West has not disproven the powers, it has simply stopped believing what the apostles plainly believed, and dressed the unbelief as maturity. Paul was not a peasant frightened of the dark. He was a trained mind writing to sophisticated cities, and he assumed a real enemy and a real war without embarrassment, and our embarrassment is a cultural inheritance we mistook for a discovery. Here is where the writer has to stand inside it, because he came to faith out of atheism and once held the closed world with both hands. He knows how obvious the flat cosmos feels, how reasonable it is to assume there is nothing behind the visible. And he knows the thing that finally cracked it, which was not a ghost story but the surplus in human evil, the way atrocity so reliably exceeds every rational motive, as if something were being served beyond the calculating self. C. S. Lewis named the two errors exactly. There are two equal and opposite mistakes our race can make about the devils, he wrote, one is to disbelieve in their existence, the other is to believe and to feel an excessive and unhealthy interest in them, and the enemy is equally pleased by both. The whole of this study lives in the narrow place between those errors. The powers are real, both personal and woven into the institutions and ideologies that outlive the people who serve them, the very thing Scripture calls principalities. The war is not a metaphor and it is not a hobby. It is being fought on a front you walk across every day, and the first act of a soldier is simply to stop pretending he is a civilian.

scriptureStudy.note: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field. The Bible introduces evil not as an abstract force but as a voice, personal and deceptive, working through a question that makes the good command sound like a cage. The war begins with a lie about God's character, and it still does.

The satan, the accuser, appears before God and is given a limited leash. Two things are held together here that the errors pull apart, that the enemy is real and active, and that he is never sovereign, never off the leash, never outside the permission and purpose of God.

We do not wrestle against flesh and blood but against the rulers and authorities and cosmic powers. Paul locates the real conflict behind the human one, ruling out the materialist who sees only flesh and blood and the superstitious man who fights only visible enemies.

The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. The enemy's chief weapon is not the dramatic manifestation but the quiet blinding, the veil over the mind that makes the gospel look dull or false. Most of his work is done in the dark, unseen and unremarked.

He was a murderer from the beginning and does not stand in the truth, for he is a liar and the father of lies. Jesus names the enemy's native language. Deception, not spectacle, is the primary front, which is exactly why materialist Christians are so easily worked, they have agreed in advance to see nothing.

Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. The image is sober and serious without being frantic. Be watchful, Peter says, not terrified, the posture of a soldier who knows there is a war and also knows who wins it.

By him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. Even the powers, in their created origin, are things Christ made and things Christ holds. The enemy commands nothing he did not first receive from the One he rebelled against.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the debate the session only gestures at, because the twentieth century produced a serious argument about what the New Testament powers actually are, and a group is served by knowing its shape. The Dutch theologian Hendrik Berkhof, in Christ and the Powers, argued that Paul's principalities are not only individual spirits but the structures and orders that govern collective human life, ideologies, traditions, institutions, which were created good, fell into rebellion, and now bind rather than serve. Walter Wink carried this much further in his trilogy on the powers, Naming the Powers, Unmasking the Powers, and Engaging the Powers, proposing that the powers are the interior spirituality of concrete institutions, the inner aspect of every outer structure, so that a corporation or a nation or a movement really does have a spirit that can turn demonic. A group should take the strong form of Wink's case, because it explains something the individualized reading misses, the way evil so often outlives every individual and takes on a life inside a system that no single person inside it intends. Then it should hear the sober critique, made by evangelical and Reformed voices such as the New Testament scholar Clinton Arnold in Powers of Darkness, that Wink tends to dissolve the personal enemy into the merely structural, demythologizing Paul until the devil becomes a sociological abstraction, and that Paul plainly means personal spiritual beings and not only the spirit of institutions. The mature verdict is not to choose. Scripture holds both, a personal enemy and the fallen structures he works through, and loses neither. Set this beside the older tradition, Augustine's two cities in The City of God, where the whole of history is the conflict of the city of God and the city of man, and the demonic works precisely through the loves and loyalties of the earthly city. The aim is to see that the war is fought at once in the individual heart and in the great structures of the age, and that a reading which keeps only one of those has already lost half the battlefield.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group is a committed rationalist by temperament, an engineer, careful and skeptical, and he says frankly that he became a Christian for the historical case for the resurrection and has always quietly regarded the language of demons and powers as embarrassing baggage he tolerates for the sake of the rest. He is not hostile, he is honest, and the session on the powers has made him uncomfortable. Here is the work for the leader, and it must honor his mind before it presses it. His skepticism is not sin, it is often a gift, and a group needs the man who refuses to be stampeded into superstition by a scary anecdote. Affirm that plainly. But notice the shape of his discomfort, because it is not the discomfort of someone who has weighed the New Testament's account of the powers and found it wanting, it is the discomfort of someone who inherited a modern frame and never examined it, who lets the resurrection through the door because it has evidence he respects and keeps the powers on the porch because they do not fit the water he was raised in. Ask him, gently, whether the same Paul he trusts on the empty tomb is a reliable enough witness to be taken seriously on the war he plainly thought he was fighting. Honor the engineer fully. Then ask him to consider that the closed world he calls maturity may be the one thing he never actually put on the test bench.

memoryVerse.text: For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.

sessions.title: The Armor of God, Piece by Piece
sessions.aim: To read Ephesians 6:10 through 18 the way Paul wrote it, as a description of the ordinary Christian life put on as armor, and to refuse both the reading that turns the armor into a magic incantation and the reading that treats it as mere metaphor with no enemy behind it.
sessions.summary: Bell says the most misread passage in all the warfare texts is the armor of God, and it gets misread in opposite directions on the same Sunday. One church treats the armor like an incantation, a checklist you recite each morning, imagining a helmet and a shield settling onto your body, as if the words themselves were the weapon. Another church treats it as a pretty metaphor for having a good attitude, the enemy long since evaporated into a figure of speech. The real question is what Paul actually says the armor is, and the answer is startling once you notice it. Every piece is something you already have in Christ and are told to put on, which means to live out. The belt is truth. The breastplate is righteousness. The shoes are the readiness of the gospel of peace. The shield is faith. The helmet is salvation. The sword, the only offensive piece, is the word of God. Paul is not describing a spell. He is describing the Christian life, worn deliberately, as the thing that actually holds under attack. Bell takes the strong case for the vivid, prayerful use of the armor, that praying through the pieces each morning is a real and ancient discipline, and grants it. He takes the strong case for the sober reading, that the armor is not a technique that makes you invincible, and grants that too. Then the turn. The command attached to the armor is not attack. Four times Paul says stand. The armor is not for conquest. It is for holding the ground Christ already won, in the evil day, until it passes.

keyScripture.why: Therefore take up the whole armor of God, that you may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand firm, naming the whole purpose of the armor as standing and not storming, holding the ground already secured rather than seizing new territory by force.

discussion.q: Bell says one church treats the armor like an incantation and another treats it as mere metaphor. Which reading did you grow up with, and how has it shaped the way you actually face temptation?
discussion.behind: Open by exposing the two distortions before repairing them. The person raised on the incantation reading recites the pieces and feels protected by the recitation. The person raised on the metaphor reading has quietly emptied the passage of any enemy. Help the room locate its own inheritance, because you cannot read the passage rightly until you see how you were taught to read it wrongly.

discussion.q: Every piece of armor is something you already have in Christ, told to put on, which means to live out. What changes when you hear the belt of truth not as a recitation but as actually telling the truth, and the breastplate of righteousness as actually living upright?
discussion.behind: Press on the central insight of the session. The armor is the Christian life worn deliberately. Help the room feel that putting on the breastplate of righteousness is not a mystical act but the concrete decision to live rightly when it is costly, so that the passage moves from magic to obedience without losing the reality of the war it is fought in.

discussion.q: The sword of the Spirit, the word of God, is the only offensive piece, and Jesus used it in the desert by answering every temptation with it is written. How well do you actually know the book you are handed as your only weapon?
discussion.behind: Bring the abstraction down to a hard, practical measure. The sword is Scripture, and Jesus wielded it not by quoting spectacularly but by knowing it well enough to answer a specific lie with a specific truth. Ask the room, without shaming, how deep their actual familiarity with Scripture runs, because a soldier who cannot find his sword in the dark is carrying it for decoration.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case for praying through the armor each morning as an old and real discipline. What is good in that practice, and where does it tip over into treating the words as the weapon?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Praying through the pieces is a genuine and ancient discipline that focuses the mind on Christ, and the leader should not sneer at it. But it tips into incantation the moment the recitation itself is felt to be the protection, rather than the life it points to. Help the room keep the discipline while refusing the superstition, which is a distinction worth naming carefully.

discussion.q: Four times in this passage Paul says stand, and never once says attack or conquer. Why do you think the command is to hold ground rather than to take it, and where have you been trying to storm what you were only asked to stand in?
discussion.behind: Close on the reframe that governs the whole session. The armor is defensive and the posture is standing, because the ground was already won at the cross. Help the room see how much exhausting Christian striving is an attempt to seize by force what we were only ever told to hold, and let the relief of that land. Standing is not passivity. It is the refusal to be moved off ground already yours.

objections.objection: The armor of God is just a memorable metaphor for being a good person. Dressing it up as literal spiritual weaponry against invisible forces is reading far too much into what is basically an inspirational word picture.
objections.response: Grant what is true, because the metaphor reading is right that the pieces are moral and spiritual, not literal brass. Paul is plainly using the image of a Roman soldier's kit, and no one is meant to feel an actual helmet. But notice what the metaphor-only reading has to ignore to stay comfortable. Paul does not introduce the armor as a word picture for self-improvement. He introduces it by saying our struggle is against rulers and authorities and cosmic powers, and then he says put on the armor so that you can stand against the schemes of the devil. The image is figurative. The war it is armor for is not. To keep the metaphor and quietly delete the enemy is to take Paul's illustration and throw away his point, which is that there is a real assault and these are the real defenses, truth and righteousness and faith and Scripture, that actually hold under it. The picture is vivid precisely because the danger is genuine.

objections.objection: I have prayed the armor of God over myself and my family many times, and I still got attacked, still fell into sin, still suffered. So either the armor does not work or I was not doing it right, and both of those are discouraging.
objections.response: Hear the discouragement, because it points at a real distortion worth clearing. If you were taught that reciting the armor makes you invincible, that the words function as a shield that stops all trouble from landing, then you were handed a superstition, and it failed you because it was never what Paul promised. Read the passage again and notice what it does not say. It does not say the armored Christian avoids the evil day. It says the armor is for the evil day, so that you may be able to stand in it, having done all, to stand. The armor is not a force field that keeps the arrows from coming, it is the equipment that keeps you on your feet while they do. You were not doing it wrong by being attacked. Being attacked is assumed. The question the passage actually asks is not whether you were hit but whether you were still standing afterward, and the belt of truth and the shield of faith are precisely what let a struck soldier remain on the ground that is already his.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which piece of the armor is the one you have quietly left off, the truth you avoid telling, the righteousness you have let slide, the faith you have stopped raising, and what has going without it cost you in the evil day?
sessions.practice: This week, take the sword seriously. Choose one lie you are actually tempted to believe, that you are worthless, that God is against you, that the sin is too strong, that no one would care, and find one specific passage of Scripture that answers it, and learn it well enough to answer without the book in your hand, the way Jesus answered in the desert. Then, when the lie comes, wield it. Write down what happens in you when you meet a specific temptation with a specific word rather than with willpower.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord, you did not send us into the evil day unarmed, and you did not hand us a spell to recite. You handed us your own truth to wear, your own righteousness to stand in, your own gospel to walk on, faith to raise against the arrows, salvation to guard the mind, and your word as the one blade we carry. Forgive us for reciting the pieces and living without them, and forgive us for keeping the picture and forgetting the war. Teach us to put on what is already ours in Christ, and having done all, simply to stand, unmoved from the ground you already won for us. Amen.
reflection: Have I treated the armor as words to recite or as a life to live, and what would it look like to actually put on the piece I keep leaving off?
How well do I really know the one offensive weapon I am given, and would I be able to answer a specific lie with a specific word if the desert came today?
Where have I been exhausting myself trying to storm and conquer what Christ already won, when the command was only to stand?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the most misread passage in all the warfare texts is the armor of God, and the remarkable thing is that it gets misread in opposite directions on the very same Sunday. In one church the armor is treated like an incantation. You recite the pieces each morning, picturing a helmet lowering onto your head and a shield strapping to your arm, and the recitation itself is felt to be the protection, as if the words were a spell that seals the day. In another church, across town, the armor has become a pretty metaphor for having a good attitude, the enemy long since evaporated into a figure of speech, the whole passage flattened into a call to be positive and kind. Both churches are reading the same paragraph, and both have missed what it plainly says. So we have to do the slow work and read it piece by piece, the way Paul wrote it, because the meaning is hiding in a detail that both distortions skip. Watch what each piece of the armor actually is. The belt is truth. The breastplate is righteousness. The shoes are the readiness given by the gospel of peace. The shield is faith. The helmet is salvation. And the sword, the single offensive weapon in the whole kit, is the word of God. Now notice the thing that changes everything. Every one of those pieces is something the Christian already has in Christ and is now commanded to put on, which is Paul's ordinary word for live out, take up, actually wear. He is not describing a magic ritual. He is describing the Christian life itself, put on deliberately, as the thing that actually holds when the assault comes. The belt of truth is telling the truth and living in reality when the enemy's whole trade is the lie. The breastplate of righteousness is living uprightly, because a life of hidden compromise has already unbuckled its own armor. The shield of faith is trust in God raised deliberately against the flaming arrows of accusation and doubt. The sword of the Spirit is Scripture, known well enough to answer with. This is why the desert matters. When Jesus was led into the wilderness to be tempted, he did not answer the enemy with spectacle or with raw power, though he had both. He answered every single temptation with it is written, and then a specific word, meeting a specific lie with a specific truth. That is the sword in a trained hand. He did not wave the Scriptures around. He knew them well enough to find the exact blade for the exact thrust, in the dark, while hungry. Take the strong case for the vivid, prayerful use of the armor, because it is old and real and Bell will not sneer at it. Praying through the pieces each morning, consciously putting on truth and righteousness and faith, is a genuine discipline that has steadied many believers and fixes the mind on Christ before the day's assaults arrive. Grant it fully. Now take the strong case for the sober reading, which is also right, that the armor is not a technique that makes you invincible, not a force field that keeps the arrows from ever landing. Grant that too, because the person who was promised invincibility and then got hit walks away thinking either the armor failed or he did, when in fact he simply believed a superstition the passage never taught. Here is where both readings get corrected by a single word, or rather by one word repeated four times. Read the passage and count how often Paul gives the command. Stand against the schemes of the devil. Withstand in the evil day. Having done all, stand. Stand therefore. Four times he says stand, and not once does he say attack, storm, conquer, or advance. The armor is almost entirely defensive, the one exception being a sword, and even the sword is for the soldier who is holding his position. This is the whole thing the sensational reading cannot abide and the sober reading needs to recover. The armor is not for conquest. The conquest already happened, at a cross, which is next week's session and the ground under this one. The armor is for holding the territory Christ already took, standing on ground that is already yours while the evil day does its worst, until the day passes. And I have to say plainly that I have spent long seasons trying to storm what I was only asked to stand in, exhausting myself in a striving God never commanded, treating the Christian life as a war of conquest I had to win rather than a position I had only to hold. The relief of the passage, once you see it, is enormous. You are not asked to defeat the enemy. He is already defeated. You are asked to put on what is already yours, and having done all, to still be standing when the smoke clears, on the same ground where the King left you.

scriptureStudy.note: Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. The whole passage opens by locating the strength outside the soldier. It is not your might that holds, which is why the armor is God's armor and not equipment you manufacture. The command to be strong is a command to lean.

Stand therefore, having fastened on the belt of truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness. Truth and righteousness are the first two pieces, and both are moral and lived, not recited. A life of hidden lies and quiet compromise has already loosened its own armor before the battle starts.

Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. The flaming darts are the accusations and doubts, and the shield is trust deliberately raised. Faith here is not a feeling but an act, lifted against a specific incoming lie.

Take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. The mind is guarded by salvation, the settled knowledge of whose you are, and the one offensive weapon is Scripture. Everything else defends. Only the word cuts.

It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. Jesus meets the first temptation with the sword, a specific word for a specific lie. He models the only offensive weapon in the kit, wielded not by volume but by knowing the text.

Be gone, Satan. For it is written, You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve. The final answer in the desert is again the sword, and the enemy leaves. Jesus does not out-argue him with cleverness, he stands on the written word and holds.

Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication. The armor passage ends not with a weapon but with prayer, the atmosphere the whole soldier breathes. The armor is worn in the posture of dependence, which is why the sword and the knees belong together.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the interpretive question the session raises, because how you read the armor depends on a decision about what the Christian life fundamentally is, and the tradition has divided in instructive ways. The biblical counselor David Powlison, in Power Encounters, argued that the New Testament frames spiritual warfare overwhelmingly in ethical and moral terms, that the way you resist the devil in the epistles is by putting off the old self and putting on the new, by truth-telling and righteousness and faith, and not by the deliverance techniques and incantations of the popular warfare movement. A group should take the strong form of Powlison's case, because it is anchored in the plain shape of Ephesians 6, where every piece of the armor is a matter of character and obedience, and it rightly rebukes the reading that turns warfare into a specialized ritual for experts. Set this beside the strong case from the other side, made by writers in the charismatic and third-wave traditions such as Clinton Arnold, who, while sober, insists that the epistles do assume real personal enemies and that prayer against them is not superstition but obedience. The mature reading holds the two together, resisting the enemy chiefly through the ordinary means of a righteous life and a raised faith, while refusing to demythologize the enemy out of existence. Then take up the older witness, Martin Luther, who wrote A Mighty Fortress Is Our God in the aftermath of plague and against a cosmos he took to be crowded with real demonic assault, and yet whose refrain is not incantation but the plain word, one little word shall fell the devil, meaning the word of God and the name of Christ. Luther held the reality of the war and the ordinariness of the weapons at once, terrified of the enemy and utterly unafraid because of the Lord. The aim is to recover the armor as neither spell nor metaphor but as the Christian life itself, put on against a real assault, and held by a strength that was never the soldier's own.
sessions.caseStudy: A woman in your group has come out of a church that taught her to pray the armor over her home every morning, naming each piece aloud and picturing it, and to bind and rebuke spirits whenever anything went wrong, a flat tire, a sick child, a bad day. She found it exhausting and finally frightening, a world of constant threat held off only by getting the words right, and she has drifted toward the opposite conclusion, that none of it was real and she can stop. Here is the work for the leader, and it must catch her before she falls off the other side of the horse. Do not simply validate her relief, because the cure for a superstition is not unbelief. Honor what was true in her old church, that there is a real enemy and that prayer against him is right and good. But name plainly what went wrong, that she was handed the armor as an incantation whose power lived in the recitation, so that the burden of protecting her family fell on getting the ritual correct, which is a weight no believer was ever meant to carry. Show her the four commands to stand, and the truth that the ground was already won. Help her see that she can lay down the frantic recitation without laying down the war, that the belt of truth and the shield of faith are a life to live and not a spell to perform, and that the outcome of the battle was never resting on whether she said the words right this morning.

memoryVerse.text: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.

sessions.title: The Enemy Within
sessions.aim: To locate the front of the battle inside the Christian and not only outside, to read temptation the way James does, as the enemy working through desires that are genuinely our own, and to refuse both the reading that blames every sin on a demon and the reading that denies any enemy at all.
sessions.summary: Bell says the great temptation in a study on spiritual warfare is to spend all your attention on the enemy out there and never once look at the enemy in here, which is exactly the arrangement the actual enemy prefers. The real question is where sin actually begins, and James answers it with brutal clarity. Each person is tempted, he writes, when he is lured and enticed by his own desire, and then desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin fully grown brings forth death. Not a demon made you do it. Your own desire did, and the enemy's genius is not to override your will but to work the field you already left unguarded. Bell takes the strong case for the deliverance reading, that some bondage is real and that the New Testament does describe deliverance, and grants it. He takes the strong case for the opposite reading, that most of what people blame on the devil is simply the flesh with a costume on, and grants that too. Then the turn, through the desert. When the enemy came for Jesus, he did not come with horns. He came with reasonable suggestions attached to real hungers, bread for a starving man, safety, a shortcut to a kingdom that was rightfully his. Temptation is not usually the offer of something obviously evil. It is the offer of something good, at the wrong time, on the enemy's terms, aimed at a desire that is already there. Which means the battle is not mainly out there. It is fought at the exact seam where a real enemy meets a real appetite, and you cannot win it by looking only outward.

keyScripture.why: But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire, then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death, naming the front of the battle inside the person and refusing to let anyone blame the enemy for a desire that was genuinely his own.

discussion.q: Bell says a warfare study tempts us to watch the enemy out there and never look at the enemy in here. Where have you found it easier to blame something outside you than to face a desire that was genuinely your own?
discussion.behind: Open on the self-implicating move that governs the whole session. It is far more comfortable to fight an external enemy than to admit that the sin grew from a desire I own. Help the room notice the reflex to externalize, without either excusing the enemy or letting anyone off the hook, and go first by naming your own version of it.

discussion.q: James says sin begins when we are lured by our own desire, not when a demon overrides our will. How does it change your fight with a besetting sin to admit that the desire behind it is actually yours?
discussion.behind: Press on the ownership. As long as the sin is someone else's fault, a demon's or a circumstance's, no repentance is possible, because you cannot repent of what you did not do. Help the room feel that owning the desire is not despair but the doorway to actually fighting it, because you can only put to death a thing you have admitted is alive in you.

discussion.q: In the desert the enemy offered Jesus good things, bread, safety, a kingdom, at the wrong time and on the wrong terms. Where is your temptation not the offer of something evil but the offer of something good aimed at a real hunger?
discussion.behind: Bring the abstraction down to the actual shape of temptation. Most temptation is not obviously wicked, it is a legitimate desire, for rest, for respect, for intimacy, for security, offered a shortcut. Help the room see their own temptations this way, which both dignifies the desire and exposes the lie, and makes the fight far more precise than a vague war on badness.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that most of what people blame on the devil is simply the flesh in a costume. What is true in that, and where might it go too far and deny a real enemy altogether?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The blame-the-flesh reading is right that we too easily externalize our own sin, and that maturity means owning it. But it can tip into denying any enemy at all, collapsing back into the materialism of session one. Help the room keep the ownership without losing the war, which is the balance the whole study is built on.

discussion.q: Jesus met each temptation not with willpower but with a specific word of Scripture aimed at the specific lie. What lie sits under your most familiar temptation, and what truth would actually answer it?
discussion.behind: Close on the practical hope. Behind every temptation is a lie about God, that he is holding out on you, that his way will not satisfy, that you must secure the good yourself. Help the room name the specific lie under a specific temptation and find the specific truth, because a vague resolve to be better has never once defeated a specific, well-aimed lie.

objections.objection: If my sin comes from my own desire, as James says, then all this talk of an enemy is beside the point. Just call it what it is, my own choices, and drop the spiritual warfare language entirely.
objections.response: Grant the ownership, because it is exactly what James insists on and what the session is built to recover. Your desire is genuinely yours, the sin is genuinely your act, and no enemy is allowed to carry the blame that belongs to you. Hold that with both hands. But notice that James is not the whole of Scripture, and even James, a few chapters later, says resist the devil and he will flee from you, so the same letter that locates sin in your desire also assumes a real enemy to resist. The two are not rivals. The enemy does not usually override your will, he works the field of your desires, sharpening a legitimate hunger into a demand, dressing a shortcut as wisdom, whispering that God is holding out on you. To drop the warfare language because sin is your own is like a soldier deciding there is no enemy because the bullet that hit him was aimed at a weakness in his own line. The desire is yours. The one who studies your desires and exploits them is not. Maturity holds both.

objections.objection: Telling people their temptations come from their own desires just heaps on shame. People already hate themselves for their struggles, and now you are saying the problem is not out there but in their own hearts.
objections.response: Hear the pastoral concern, because it is real and the fear of shame is not foolish. But consider what the alternative actually offers. If your desires are not yours, if the problem is only an external enemy to be bound and rebuked, then you are never the agent of your own life, and you are also never able to genuinely change, because you cannot put to death what you refuse to admit is alive. Owning the desire is not the same as hating yourself. It is the first honest act of a person who wants to be free. And notice where the ownership sits in the gospel, not at the end as a verdict but at the beginning as a diagnosis, followed immediately by the news that this very self, desires and all, has been crucified with Christ and is being remade. The shame reading assumes that to name the desire is to condemn the person. The gospel names the desire precisely so it can be dealt with rather than managed, and offers not a rebuke but a death and a resurrection. You do not have to choose between honesty about your heart and hope for it. The cross gives you both.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What good and legitimate desire has the enemy learned to use against you, and what shortcut does he keep offering that you keep taking?
sessions.practice: This week, take your most familiar temptation and trace it backward past the act to the desire underneath, and past the desire to the lie about God that makes the shortcut feel reasonable. Name the good thing you were really after, name the lie that promised it the wrong way, and find the word that answers the lie. Do not fight the act with willpower. Fight the lie with the truth, the way Jesus did in the desert. Write down what you find at the bottom of the temptation, because it is almost never what you assumed.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we would rather fight an enemy out there than face the desire in here, and the real enemy is glad to let us. Forgive us for blaming him for what our own hearts wanted, and forgive us for pretending there was no enemy at all when he was working the very field we left unguarded. You know the good hungers we carry and the shortcuts we keep taking. Meet us at the seam where the lie touches the appetite, and put your true word in our mouths there, the way your Son answered in the desert. We cannot win this by watching only the door. Do the deeper work inside. Amen.
reflection: Where have I found it easier to blame an enemy, or a circumstance, than to own the desire that actually gave birth to the sin?
What legitimate hunger has the enemy learned to exploit in me, and what shortcut does he keep offering it?
What is the specific lie about God that sits under my most familiar temptation, and do I know the specific truth that answers it?
sessions.teaching: Bell says the great danger of a study like this one is that it lets you spend all your attention on the enemy out there and never once look at the enemy in here, which is precisely the arrangement the actual enemy would choose if you asked him. A Christian obsessed with binding demons over his house and utterly unwilling to examine the desires in his own chest is a Christian the enemy can work with for years. So this session turns the lens around, from the powers outside to the front inside, and it turns to the one writer in the New Testament who is most brutally clear about where sin actually begins. James refuses every excuse in a single sentence. Each person is tempted, he says, when he is lured and enticed by his own desire, and then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin, and sin, when it is fully grown, brings forth death. Read that slowly, because it dismantles the whole apparatus of blame. Not a demon made you do it. Not your circumstances, not your upbringing, not the culture, though all of those are real. Your own desire did. The metaphor James reaches for is conception and birth, which means the sin is not something done to you from outside, it is something conceived inside you, carried, and delivered. This is the ownership that no honest fight can skip, and it is the exact thing the sensational reading of warfare quietly avoids. If every sin is a demon's doing, then I am never the one who did it, and a person who never did anything can never repent of anything. But watch, because the sober reading has its own cliff on the other side. If James is the whole story, if sin is only ever my own flesh and there is no enemy at all, then we have simply walked back into the closed world of session one, and we have to explain away James himself, who in the very same letter says resist the devil and he will flee from you. So the same short book insists that the desire is yours and that the enemy is real, and it feels no tension between the two. Here is how they fit, and the desert shows it better than any argument. When the enemy came for Jesus in the wilderness, he did not come with horns and a pitchfork. He came with reasonable suggestions, and every one of them was attached to a real and legitimate hunger. Turn these stones to bread, he said, to a man who had not eaten in forty days, and hunger is not a sin, and bread is not evil, and Jesus could rightly have eaten. Throw yourself down and let the angels catch you, he said, and the desire to be spectacularly vindicated is a real pull in every human heart. Bow to me and take all the kingdoms, he said, offering by shortcut the very kingdoms that were in fact rightfully Christ's to inherit. This is the anatomy of temptation, and it is almost never the offer of something obviously evil. It is the offer of something good, at the wrong time, on the enemy's terms, aimed with precision at a desire that is already there. The enemy does not usually manufacture new appetites in you. He studies the ones you already have and offers them a crooked path. Which means the battle is fought at a seam, the exact place where a real enemy meets a real appetite, and you cannot win it by watching only the door. Take the strong case for the deliverance reading, honestly, because it is not nothing. Some bondage is real, the New Testament does describe deliverance, and Bell will not pretend the Gospels are silent about people genuinely held. Grant it. Now take the strong case for the other reading, that most of what modern Christians blame on the devil is simply the flesh wearing a costume, an ordinary sin dignified with a spiritual name so the sinner can avoid the mirror. Grant that too, and grant that it is more often the problem in a comfortable church than active possession. And here is where the writer has to climb inside the indictment, because I have done exactly this. I have named a struggle a spiritual attack when it was plainly my own appetite, dressed my compromise in warfare language so that I could fight the enemy instead of repenting of myself. The enemy was delighted to be blamed. It kept me busy at the door while the real damage was being done in the kitchen. So hear the thing this session is finally after. Jesus won the desert not with raw power, which he had, and not with willpower, but by answering each lie with a specific truth, it is written, aimed exactly where the lie was aimed. Behind every temptation is a lie about God, that he is holding out on you, that his way will not satisfy the hunger, that you had better secure the good thing yourself because he will not. The fight is not mainly against the act. It is against the lie under the act, at the seam where the enemy meets your own true desire, and it is won the way it was won in the wilderness, with the truth about God held in the mouth against the lie.

scriptureStudy.note: Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God, for God tempts no one. James closes off the first excuse, that God set me up. Temptation is not from above, which forces the question of where it does come from, and James answers with the human heart, not only the enemy.

Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. The words are drawn from hunting and fishing, a bait and a hook. The enemy supplies the hook, but the bait works only because the desire is already yours. He cannot lure you with a hunger you do not have.

If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread. The first temptation targets a real hunger after forty days of fasting, and questions Jesus's identity. Temptation nearly always begins with if, a doubt slipped under a legitimate need.

To you I will give all this authority, if you will worship me. The enemy offers the kingdoms by a shortcut, the very kingdoms Christ came to inherit by the cross. The offer is not of something false but of something true, secured the wrong way, which is the pattern of nearly every temptation.

You will be like God, knowing good and evil. The first temptation was not a craving for something ugly but a reach for something exalted, likeness to God, offered by a lie that God was withholding it. The oldest bait is the suggestion that God is holding out on you.

Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. Paul names the internal war directly, the flesh against the Spirit, and the front is inside the believer. The enemy exploits this field but does not create it. The flesh is our own.

Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. The order is the wisdom. Submission to God comes first, and only the submitted person can resist, because resistance is not raw willpower but the turning of a surrendered heart against the lie.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the long tradition of thought about temptation, because the church has mapped this inner terrain with a care the modern warfare industry rarely matches. The desert fathers, and later the monastic tradition catalogued by writers such as Evagrius and John Cassian, studied the logismoi, the intrusive thoughts, tracing how a temptation moves from a first suggestion through engagement to consent, and insisting that the early stage, the mere arrival of the thought, is not yet sin, but that the entertaining of it is where the will begins to turn. A group can weigh this against James, noticing how precisely the ancient map matches his sequence of desire, conception, and birth, and how both refuse to let the arrival of a temptation be confused with the guilt of a sin. Set this beside Augustine's Confessions, where the theft of the pears becomes a study in a desire that wanted the wrong thing precisely because it was forbidden, the will curved in on itself, and notice how Augustine locates the trouble not in an external enemy but in a disordered love. Then take up the secular account at its strongest and test it. Modern psychology describes habit loops, cue and craving and reward, and the neuroscience of addiction with real accuracy, and a group should grant that this describes the mechanism of the flesh with genuine insight, common grace naming the how. But it cannot name the what, the lie about God at the bottom of the craving, nor supply the cure, which is not merely a rewired loop but a crucified and risen self. The aim is to hold the ancient wisdom, the biblical diagnosis, and the modern description together, letting each name what it can see, and to recover the fight against temptation as a fight at the seam where a real enemy, a real appetite, and a real lie about God all meet, won not by willpower but by the truth held in the mouth against the lie.
sessions.caseStudy: A man in your group has struggled for years with a hidden habit, and he speaks about it entirely in the language of attack. It comes over him, he says, it ambushes him, the enemy hits him when he is weak, and he has spent years praying for deliverance from what he experiences as an assault from outside. He is sincere, and there may well be a real enemy involved, and the leader must not mock his language. Here is the careful work. Do not simply tell him it is all his own flesh, because that can crush a man already exhausted, and because the enemy may indeed be exploiting the field. But notice what the attack language lets him avoid, which is ownership, and therefore repentance, and therefore any real fight, because a man forever waiting to be delivered from an ambush never turns to face the desire that keeps opening the gate. Gently walk him back with James, from the act to the desire, and ask what good and legitimate hunger the habit is a crooked path toward, for comfort, for escape, for a moment of feeling wanted. Help him see that owning the desire is not defeat but the first honest step toward freedom, that he cannot put to death a thing he insists was never alive in him. Honor the reality of the enemy fully. Then hand him back the responsibility the attack language had quietly taken away, not as a burden but as the only ground on which he can actually stand and fight.

memoryVerse.text: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

sessions.title: The Victory Already Won
sessions.aim: To ground the whole battle in the finished work of the cross, where Christ disarmed the powers, and to refuse both the reading that treats the war as still undecided and the reading that treats the enemy as already so gone he need not be resisted at all.
sessions.summary: Bell says every discouraged Christian in the warfare fight is fighting for victory, and every mature one is fighting from it, and the whole difference is a single event in the past tense. The real question is whether the outcome of the war is still in doubt, and the New Testament answers with a verb that is already finished. On the cross, Paul says, God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in Christ. Not will disarm. Disarmed. The decisive battle is not ahead of us, it is behind us, fought and won at a place that looked to every watching power like a defeat, a bleeding man on a Roman cross. That is the scandal at the center of Christian warfare, that the enemy was beaten not by superior force but by a death, the way a chess game is decided many moves before the board is cleared. Bell takes the strong case for taking the ongoing battle seriously, that the New Testament plainly still commands resistance, and grants it fully. He takes the strong case for the finished victory, that Christ's triumph is complete and the enemy is a defeated power throwing what is left, and grants that too. Then the turn. We live in the strange interval the New Testament assumes, between the decisive victory and its final enforcement, the already and the not yet, where the enemy is genuinely beaten and genuinely still dangerous, like a defeated army that has not yet heard, or has heard and refuses, the terms of surrender. The Christian does not fight to win. The Christian fights because the winning is done, and the resistance is the enforcement of a verdict already handed down.

keyScripture.why: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him, naming the cross as the place the powers were already defeated, so that every battle now is fought from a victory already won and not toward one still in doubt.

discussion.q: Bell says the discouraged Christian fights for victory and the mature one fights from it. Which have you been doing, and how would you know the difference in an actual hard week?
discussion.behind: Open on the reframe that governs everything. Fighting for victory means the outcome still feels in doubt, and every failure feels like it might tip the war. Fighting from victory means the outcome is settled and failures are real but not decisive. Help the room locate honestly which posture they actually live in, because most Christians affirm the finished victory and fight as if it were still up for grabs.

discussion.q: Paul says Christ disarmed the powers, past tense, at the cross. What does it do to your fear of the enemy to hear that the decisive battle is behind you and not ahead of you?
discussion.behind: Press on the tense. The whole weight of the session is in a completed verb. Help the room feel the difference between an enemy who might yet win and an enemy who has already lost and is throwing what remains. Fear assumes the outcome is open. The cross closed it. Let the relief of that land without letting it tip into carelessness.

discussion.q: The enemy was defeated not by superior force but by a death on a cross that looked like total defeat. Why do you think God chose to win the war by apparent losing, and what does that pattern say about how his victories usually look?
discussion.behind: Move to the scandal at the center. The powers were beaten by the one thing they were sure meant they had won, the execution of the King. Help the room see that God's victories often look like defeats from the inside, which reframes their own apparent losses, and guards against a triumphalism that expects the battle to always feel like winning.

discussion.q: Bell takes the strong case that the New Testament still plainly commands resistance, and the strong case that the victory is already complete. How do you hold both without tipping into either despair or carelessness?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves, which is the whole discipline of the already and the not yet. Tip too far toward not yet and you fight in fear as if it might be lost. Tip too far toward already and you grow careless as if there were nothing to resist. Help the room feel the tension as the truth rather than a problem to solve, because both errors are common and both are pastorally costly.

discussion.q: If the enemy is a defeated power throwing what is left, then his main weapon now is the lie that he has not lost. Where has he been working on you with that particular lie, that the outcome is still in doubt?
discussion.behind: Close on the enemy's actual strategy in the interval. A defeated foe who cannot win the war fights to make you believe he still can, because a Christian who thinks the outcome is open fights in fear and is far easier to discourage. Help the room name where they have believed the lie of an undecided war, and answer it with the finished verb of the cross.

objections.objection: If Christ already won and the enemy is already disarmed, then why does evil still obviously rule so much of the world? A victory that leaves the world looking exactly like a war zone is not much of a victory.
objections.response: Take the objection seriously, because it names the hardest fact honestly and Scripture does not flinch from it either. The world plainly still groans, the enemy plainly still does damage, and any account that pretends otherwise is lying to you. But consider the shape of the answer the New Testament actually gives, which is not that the victory is incomplete but that its enforcement is not yet finished. The decisive battle can be won long before the last shot is fired, the way a war can be effectively decided at a single engagement while the fighting drags on for months as the losing side refuses or has not yet heard the terms. Scripture calls this the already and the not yet. The kingdom has come in Christ and has not yet come in full. So the continuing damage is not evidence that Christ did not win, it is the death throes of a power that has lost and will not concede, and the promise is not that the war zone is an illusion but that it is temporary, that the disarmed enemy is being put finally beneath the feet of the King. A victory that still has casualties is not therefore a false victory. It is a real one, not yet fully enforced.

objections.objection: Focusing on the cross as a past victory makes Christians passive. If it is all already done, why bother resisting anything? Just relax and wait for heaven.
objections.response: Hear the worry, because a lazy triumphalism is a real distortion and the New Testament guards against it directly. But notice that the finished victory does not remove the command to resist, it grounds it. The same Paul who says the powers were disarmed at the cross is the one who says put on the armor and stand, and the same letter that announces the triumph tells you to put to death what is earthly in you. The victory is not an excuse for passivity, it is the reason resistance is not hopeless. A soldier enforcing a surrender that has already been signed does not fight less than one whose war is still in doubt, he fights differently, without fear and without the despair that comes from thinking every skirmish might lose the whole thing. The finished work turns frantic striving into steady standing. You do not resist in order to win. You resist because the winning is done, and your standing is the enforcement of a verdict already handed down, which is not passivity but the most confident kind of action there is.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Where have you been fighting for a victory that was already won, exhausting yourself trying to secure an outcome the cross already secured, and what would change if you truly believed it was finished?
sessions.practice: This week, when the enemy's discouragement comes, the lie that you are losing, that the sin is too strong, that the outcome is in doubt, answer it out loud with the finished verb. He disarmed the powers. It is finished. Do not argue the enemy into the ground on his own terms. Simply stand on the accomplished fact of the cross and refuse to fight for what Christ already won. Write down what happens to a familiar discouragement when you meet it not with more effort but with the announcement that the war is already decided.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, on the cross you looked to every watching power like a defeated man, and you were disarming them the whole time, triumphing over them in the very place they were sure they had won. We have been fighting for a victory you already secured, exhausting ourselves to win a war you finished, believing the enemy's oldest lie, that the outcome is still in doubt. Forgive us. Steady us in the strange interval where you are already Lord and not yet visibly so. Teach us to fight from your triumph and not toward it, to stand as those enforcing a verdict already handed down, unafraid because the decisive battle is behind us and the last enemy is already under your feet. Amen.
reflection: Have I been fighting for victory or from it, and where would an honest look at my fears reveal that I still think the outcome is in doubt?
Do I really believe the tense of Colossians 2:15, that Christ has already disarmed the powers, or do I live as if the decisive battle were still ahead?
Where has the enemy been working on me with his last real weapon, the lie that he has not actually lost?
sessions.teaching: Bell says that if you watch Christians in the warfare fight long enough you notice two kinds, and the difference between them is not effort and not sincerity but a single event held in a single tense. The discouraged Christian is fighting for victory, straining toward an outcome that still feels in doubt, so that every failure lands like it might tip the whole war. The mature Christian is fighting from victory, standing on an outcome already secured, so that failures are real and grievous but never decisive. And the entire difference between those two people is whether they actually believe what Paul says happened at the cross. So this session goes to the center of the whole study, the place everything else has been leaning toward, and it goes to a verb. Writing to the Colossians, Paul says that God, in Christ, disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him. Read the tense, because the tense is the gospel. Not will disarm. Not is in the process of disarming. Disarmed. The decisive battle in the war we have been describing is not somewhere ahead of us. It is behind us. It has already been fought, and it has already been won, and it was won at a place that looked, to every watching power in heaven and on earth, like the most total defeat imaginable, a bleeding man nailed to a Roman cross, abandoned, mocked, and killed. That is the scandal at the dead center of Christian warfare, and it is why this faith wins its wars in a way no other story would dare to script. The powers did not lose to superior force. They lost to a death. They threw everything they had at the Son of God and killed him, and in the very act they were sure was their triumph, they were being disarmed, publicly, the way a defeated general is stripped of his sword and marched through the streets behind the victor's chariot. Paul's image is exactly that, a triumphal procession, the conquered powers led in Christ's train. The cross was not the moment the enemy won. It was the moment he was paraded as the loser he had become. Now take the strong case for the ongoing battle, because it is plainly biblical and Bell will not soften it. The New Testament, after the cross and after the resurrection, still commands resistance, still says put on the armor, still says be watchful because the lion prowls, still assumes a real and dangerous enemy. Grant every word of it. The war is not over in the sense that no shots are fired. And now take the strong case for the finished victory, which is equally biblical, that Christ's triumph is complete, that the enemy is a defeated power and not a live contender, that the outcome is not in the balance. Grant that too. The New Testament holds both without embarrassment, and it holds them in a phrase theologians have worn smooth, the already and the not yet. The kingdom has already come in Christ. It has not yet come in full. We live in the interval between the decisive victory and its final enforcement, and everything about how a Christian fights depends on understanding where in the war we actually stand. Think of a war whose outcome is settled at a single great battle, after which the losing side is finished, its power broken, the end certain, and yet the fighting drags on for months because the defeated army has not yet heard, or has heard and refuses, the terms of its surrender. That is the interval we live in. The enemy is genuinely beaten and genuinely still dangerous, a defeated power throwing what is left of his strength precisely because he has nothing left to gain and nothing left to lose. And here is where I have to stand inside it, because I have spent long stretches of my own life fighting for a victory that was already won, straining and striving as if the whole thing might yet be lost, exhausting myself to secure an outcome the cross secured two thousand years ago. The enemy was happy to let me. His single most effective weapon now, in the interval, is not raw power, which he no longer has, but a lie, the lie that he has not actually lost, that the war is still up for grabs, that the outcome depends on how hard you fight. Because a Christian who believes the outcome is undecided fights in fear, and a frightened soldier is easy to discourage, easy to exhaust, easy to convince that the next failure will be the one that loses everything. So hear the thing this session is finally for. The answer to that lie is not more effort. It is the finished verb. He disarmed the powers. It is finished. The Christian does not fight in order to win. The winning is done, sealed at the cross, ratified at the empty tomb, and every act of resistance now is not an attempt to secure the verdict but the enforcement of a verdict already handed down. That is why the mature Christian can be at once utterly serious about the battle and utterly unafraid in it. He is not defending a fortress that might fall. He is standing on ground the King already took, holding it in the King's name, until the day the last defeated power is finally, visibly, put under his feet.

scriptureStudy.note: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him. The image is a Roman triumph, the conquered enemy stripped and paraded behind the victor. The cross, which looked like Christ's defeat, was the enemy's public humiliation.

He shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel. The first promise after the fall already names the pattern, the serpent crushed at the cost of a wound to the deliverer. The whole war and its outcome are foretold in the same breath as the first defeat.

That through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil. The weapon that defeats the enemy is death itself, Christ's own, which turns the enemy's chief instrument into the means of his undoing. He is beaten with his own sword.

The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil. The purpose is stated plainly and in the completed sense of the incarnation's aim. Christ did not come merely to teach or to comfort but to undo the enemy's work at its root.

Now is the judgment of this world, now will the ruler of this world be cast out. Jesus, on the eve of the cross, names the very hour of his apparent defeat as the hour the ruler of this world is thrown down. The losing was the winning.

The accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, and they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb. The enemy's role is accuser, and the ground of his defeat is the blood of the Lamb, so the victory is enforced not by our strength but by pleading the cross.

The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The already and the not yet in one sentence, the crushing is certain and still future, and it is under your feet, the enforcement shared with the church that stands in the finished victory.

sessions.goingDeeper: Press into the way the church has understood what the cross did to the powers, because the reading matters and the tradition has held it in a particular shape. The theme that Christ's death was a victory over the enemy is ancient, and the twentieth-century Swedish theologian Gustaf Aulen, in Christus Victor, argued that this was in fact the earliest and most characteristic way the church understood the atonement, that the cross was first of all a divine conquest of the powers of sin, death, and the devil, before the later theories of the West framed it primarily in legal terms. A group should take the strong form of Aulen's case, because it recovers a note the modern Western church often mutes, that the cross is not only a payment but a triumph, not only a courtroom but a battlefield. It should also hear the caution from Reformed and evangelical readers, that Christus Victor is best held alongside, not instead of, the truth that the cross also bore the penalty of sin, since it is precisely by bearing the legal claim against us that Christ leaves the accuser nothing left to accuse, which is why Colossians 2 sets the disarming of the powers right beside the canceling of the record of debt. The two belong together.
